body: A man of fifty-five is sitting in his brother’s front room on a Sunday afternoon with a mug of tea going cold beside him. His brother is explaining what he ought to do — the letter he should write, the solicitor he should ring on Monday, the thing he should have said in March and can still say now. It is good advice, better than anything the man has come up with himself, and given by somebody who has plainly thought about it all week. He agrees with all of it. He says yes, and yes, and that is worth doing. He has no intention of doing any of it, and on the drive home he feels worse than he did on the way over.

Everything said in that room was correct. That is what makes the afternoon hard to describe, because there is nothing to complain of and nobody to blame, and yet a man went home having been helped and arrived feeling worse than when he set out.

Advice assumes a solvable problem. Given the facts, here is the action, and if you take it the situation improves. Most of life really is like that, which is why there is so much advice about, and most of the time it is useful.

Wisdom is the older category and it is doing a different job. In Scripture the word is not first applied to a sage; it is applied to a craftsman. The men who furnished the tabernacle were filled with wisdom, meaning they could work gold and cut stone and weave — skill that lives in the hands and cannot be handed over by being explained. That sense carries into the wisdom books. They are not a stock of answers. They are training in how to be a person while a thing is true: what to hold on to, what to stop demanding, what is yours to carry. Proverbs is largely about competence. Ecclesiastes and Job sit beside it saying, and here is what to do when competence is not the issue.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations. Teaching and prayer hold frequencies of their own on it, and not every one of them is trying to get a listener to an action point before the hour is out.

Programming that way is harder than it sounds, because the pressure at every point is to be useful. An hour that ends without a step in it feels like an hour that failed, and the temptation is to reach for one simply to close the thing off. Job’s friends gave superb advice for seven days after they stopped sitting with him in silence. The silence was the wise part, and it is the part nobody remembers, because a week of saying nothing does not look like ministry and cannot be written up afterwards.

Almost everything around us now assumes solvability. There is a protocol for grief with stages in it, a framework for burnout, five steps for a difficult conversation, and an industry selling certainty about outcomes it does not control. None of this is malicious and much of it helps. But when the apparatus meets a situation that will not move, it cannot admit as much, so it changes the subject to the person: if the method works and you are still suffering, the remaining variable is you. That is how help becomes an accusation with nobody intending it, and why a certain kind of sufferer stops answering the phone.

So the material on those frequencies is arranged differently. Longer passages, read whole rather than mined for the useful verse. The lament psalms left in, including the ones that end badly, because a psalter with the complaints taken out is no use to anybody in trouble. Slower music between, with enough space that nobody is being moved along. It is programmed on the assumption that some of the audience will not be all right by Friday, and that this is not a fault in them.
None of which is an argument against advice. It is an argument about knowing which room you are in.

Be fair to advice first, because it is the greater part of what anybody needs. Most problems are ordinary and most of them yield. A checklist has saved more lives than any amount of sitting quietly ever will, and a person stuck for want of a plan should be handed a plan and not a silence. But watch what happens when the same instinct is carried into a room where nothing will change — the settled diagnosis, the estrangement where you have already apologised twice, the work you are good at and cannot continue. The advice keeps arriving, because the giver cannot bear the alternative, and it lands as an insult. It treats as a puzzle a thing the person worked out long ago is not one.
Advice offered to somebody whose situation will not change is not help. It is a bill.

On a Saturday morning a man lets himself into a friend’s house with a bag of shopping, because he knows where the key is and the friend has not answered the phone in eight days. There has been a death — a baby, at thirty-six weeks. He puts the milk in the fridge and the bread in the bin, because the bread already in there has gone. His friend comes downstairs and sits at the other end of the sofa. They watch forty minutes of a football match neither of them is following. He washes up what is in the sink, says he will come again on Tuesday, and goes. He has not said one useful thing all morning and he knows it.
That is the whole visit. What arrived in that house was not a solution and not a word. It was a person, staying a while, with no plan for the situation and no need to be seen to have one.

This is unsatisfying, and it would be dishonest to make it sound otherwise. A station that will not tell you what to do can feel like one that has withheld something. There are listeners who come to religious radio precisely for instructions and who will find this evasive, or worse, pious about being evasive. And silence is not automatically wise. A great deal of it is cowardice, or the awkwardness of people who cannot face the house and send a card instead.

The difference is attendance. Job’s friends were not wise because they were quiet; they were wise because they came, and travelled, and sat down on the ground with him for a week. That is silence with somebody in it, which is the opposite of the silence of a street that has stopped ringing. They failed only when they opened their mouths, and what came out was excellent, and it was excellent about a situation they had not troubled to understand. The seven days were not the preamble to the ministry. The seven days were the ministry.

So a wisdom frequency is not a slower advice frequency. It is a different activity, aimed at the hours after the advice has run out — which, for anybody who lives long enough, is most of the serious hours there are. It cannot hand you an action and does not pretend to. What it can do is keep company in the part of life that has no next step, and let the older books speak, written by people in exactly that position and never edited afterwards to sound more encouraging.
All of which is theory until something is playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Four kinds of programming sit on this dial. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe to have on in a room with children in it. And there are the international frequencies, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards. Nothing here asks you to describe your situation before it will play.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 313.80 — The Ancient Paths. It is Middle Eastern worship, built on the maqam, with a great deal of acoustic lament in it, and it is the closest thing on the dial to the sound the wisdom books came out of. A maqam is in no hurry to resolve. It will sit inside a phrase, turn it, leave it, come back to it, and an ear trained on four chords and a lift finds this uncomfortable for ten minutes and then stops minding. It is music that knows how to remain in an unfinished place without pretending the place is finished, which is the skill this article has been describing. Its evening hour is called Evening Maqam. Put it on and do not wait for the lift.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than a recommendation, because a recommendation is a small piece of advice and this article has spent long enough on those. Do not put HM 313.80 on to fix anything. Put it on in the room where the thing you cannot fix is, leave it running for seven days, and let it be the sort of company that does not require an answer. That is all the friends of Job got right, and it was the only week they were any use to him.
